{{nihongo|'''Amanoiwatate Shrine'''|天石立神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Yamato Province]].

'''Amanoiwatate Shrine''' (Amano-iwatate Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in the Iwatodani area of Yagyū-chō, {{ill|Nara (city)|Q169134|qid=Q169134}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287}}. It is situated in the mountains at an elevation of 330 {{ill|Metre|Q11573|qid=Q11573}}, on the northern foot of a small hill called Toiwazan. The shrine has no {{ill|Honden|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994}}; instead, it enshrines and directly worships a massive rock at which it is believed to reside. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} listed in the '{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}' as “'''Amano no Iwatate Shrine''',” and its former shrine rank was {{ill|Son-sha|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284}}.

It is said to have been a place of training for the {{ill|Yagyū clan|Q2975395|qid=Q2975395|lt=Yagyū family}} <ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://narashikanko.or.jp/wp-content/themes/nara-portal/pdf/pamphlet_pdf/yagyukaido.pdf|title=Yagyū Kaidō Walking Guidebook|date=|publisher=Nara City Nara Brand Promotion Division|accessdate=2022-09-11}}</ref>.

The area around the shrine is called Toiwadani and is a scenic spot where giant rocks and boulders are piled up one after another, including the “Ittō-seki (One-Cut Stone),” which is said to have inspired {{ill|Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba|Q24862683|qid=Q24862683}}. It was counted as one of the “Ten Scenic Views of Yagyū” by {{ill|Takuan Sōhō|Q632866|qid=Q632866|lt=Takuan}}, and was named “Mannenkei” <ref name="県史民俗">‘History of Nara Prefecture’, Vol. 13.</ref>.

=== Enshrined deities ===
{{Right|
[[File:Amanoiwatate-jinja03s6s4592.jpg|thumb|none|200px|Mae-tate-iwa (left) and Ushiro-tate-iwa]]
[[File:Amanoiwatate-jinja06s6s4592.jpg|thumb|none|200px|Mae-fuse-iwa (left) and Mae-tate-iwa]]
[[File:Amanoiwatate-jinja07s5s4592.jpg|thumb|none|200px|Kinchaku Rock (left) and Mae-fuse-iwa]]

Around three massive {{ill|Granite|Q41177|qid=Q41177}} rocks split into three door-like parts—“Mae-fuse-iwa,” “Mae-tate-iwa,” and “Ushiro-tate-iwa”—{{ill|Shimenawa|Q1887421|qid=Q1887421}} ropes are strung through the trees, and these rocks are enshrined as {{ill|Shintai|Q327532|qid=Q327532}} (sacred bodies). “Mae-tate-iwa” is also called “Kanbe (Kambe) Rock,” and together with the other two rocks is said to be a door stone that fell from the {{ill|Amano-Iwato|Q3231835|qid=Q3231835}}. In addition, a round rock called “Kinchaku Rock,” which fell from the southwestern cliff in {{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 28 ({{ill|1953|Q18585|qid=Q18585}}), is also enshrined.

;Ushiro-tate-iwa
:The shintai rock of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kushiiwamado no Mikoto}}, also called “Amano-Iwasui Shrine.” Plate-shaped.
;Mae-fuse-iwa
:The shintai rock of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amano-Iwato-wake no Mikoto}}, also called “Amatate Shrine.” Plate-shaped; height 1.2 m, width approx. 7 m, thickness 1.2 m.
;Kinchaku Rock
:The shintai rock of '''Amaterasu Ōhirume no Mikoto''' ({{ill|Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qid=Q455602}}), also called “Hyūga Shrine.” Round-shaped; width 7 m, height 7 m.
The enshrined deities of each rock are based on ‘Gyokuei Shūi’, and the site is noted as an excellent example of ancient It is also said that each of the giant stones distributed throughout the entire area of the shrine is inhabited by all 3,123 deities.

=== Origins ===
This is an ancient shrine that preserves a primordial form of ritual worship in which the giant rocks themselves are revered as shintai, with no main hall, and the date of its founding is unknown <ref>‘Shikinaisha Research Report’.</ref>. Giant rocks can be seen everywhere extending toward Mount Toiwa behind the shrine, and in the mountainous areas of Nara City, including Yagyū, there are many traces of faith centered on giant rocks and boulders. For example, Tateban Shrine, a {{ill|Sessha|Q135009904|qid=Q135009904}} of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yashifuyamaguchi Shrine}} in Ōyagyū-chō, is also built atop a giant rock.

In the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, the ‘Engishiki Jinmyōchō’ lists it as a minor shrine, and according to shrine tradition, it was founded in ancient times based on the legend of the Amano-Iwato. That is, when {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tajikarao no Mikoto}} opened the Amano-Iwato, the door stone is said to have flown to this place, and from the meaning “the door of the divine dwelling,” it came to be called “Kanbe Rock” <ref name="県史民俗"/><ref>‘Ganyōki’ (a work by shrine priests of Kasuga Taisha in the early modern period) records a similar tradition, stating that the Ise Great Deity is enshrined in the center, Kasuga Daimyōjin on the left, and Tajikarao Myōjin on the right.</ref>. The area was later donated as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shrine land}} to {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|ca|Gran santuari de Kasuga|co|Grandi Santuariu Kasuga|cs|Svatyně Kasuga|de|Kasuga-Taisha|es|Kasuga-taisha|eu|Kasuga-taisha|fa|کاسوگا-تایشا|fi|Kasuga-taisha|fr|Kasuga-taisha|he|מקדש קאסוגה|id|Kuil Agung Kasuga|it|Santuario Kasuga|ja|春日大社|ka|კასუგა-ტაისია|ko|가스가타이샤|la|Kasuga-taisha|pl|Kasuga Taisha|pt|Kasuga-taisha|ru|Касуга тайся|sh|Kasuga-taisha|simple|Kasuga Taisha|sl|Svetišče Kasuga|th|ศาลเจ้าคาซูงะ|tok|tomo sewi suli Kasuka|tr|Kasuga-taisha|uk|Касуга тайся|zh|春日大社|qid=Q714559}} during the time of {{ill|kampaku|Q1199966|qid=Q1199966}} {{ill|Fujiwara no Yorimichi|Q1370620|qid=Q1370620}}, and it is said that Kanbe Rock resounded at that time. Until the early modern period, it reportedly continued to resound whenever there was an auspicious event in the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|Q909452|qid=Q909452}} <ref>‘Kanbe Rock Origins’.</ref>.

It is said that {{ill|Yagyū Munetoshi|Q724287|qid=Q724287}} (Yagyū Sekishūsai) practiced swordsmanship at this shrine, and during the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, it was revered by successive lords of the {{ill|Yagyū Domain|Q10863542|qid=Q10863542}}. Stone lanterns inscribed with {{ill|Hōei|Q1145262|qid=Q1145262}} 2 ({{ill|1705|Q6830|qid=Q6830}}), donated by Yagyū Munehiro ({{ill|Yagyū Toshikata|Q11534512|qid=Q11534512|lt=Toshikata}}), and those inscribed with {{ill|Kanpō|Q1145798|qid=Q1145798}} 2 ({{ill|1742|Q7575|qid=Q7575}}) by {{ill|Yagyū Toshihira|Q10729347|qid=Q10729347|lt=Toshihira}} remain. At {{ill|Hōtoku-ji Temple|Q11615783|qid=Q11615783}}, the {{ill|Bodaiji|Q1084697|qid=Q1084697}} of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yagyū family}}, there is preserved an origin text of this shrine, ‘Kanbe Rock Origins,’ with a {{ill|Bodaiji|Q1084697|qid=Q1084697}} dated {{ill|Kan'ei|Q1192913|qid=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|1625|Q6826|qid=Q6826}}).

In the {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}}, it was ranked as a village shrine, but in the ‘{{ill|jinjameisaichou|Q11590704|qid=Q11590704}}’ of the same year 7 ({{ill|1874|Q7761|qid=Q7761}}), it was listed as “Toiwadani Shrine.”

=== Rituals ===
There is a custom called “Mawari Kannushi,” in which the role of {{ill|Kannushi (disambiguation)|Q15888735|qid=Q15888735}} is taken in rotation among the districts of Yagyū-chō. The person serving as priest is responsible for replacing the shimenawa on the shintai rocks at {{ill|Japanese New Year|Q701398|qid=Q701398}}, but during ordinary times, the {{ill|miyaza|Q11454763|qid=Q11454763}} of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yasaka Shrine}} takes care of the shrine <ref name="白水社">‘Gods of Japan’.</ref>.

=== Shrine buildings ===
As mentioned above, the shrine has no main hall; only a simple tiled-roof worship hall stands to the east of the shintai rocks, beside Kinchaku Rock. Between the shintai rocks and the worship hall stand two stone lanterns donated by the lords of the Yagyū Domain. In the past, a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Noh stage}} built by Munehiro (Toshikata) in Hōei 2 was also installed, but it has since been relocated to Yasaka Shrine in Yagyū-chō and is used in place of that shrine’s worship hall.

=== Ittō-seki (One-Cut Stone) ===
[[File:Amanoiwatate-jinja10s5s3200.jpg|thumb|200px|Ittō-seki]]
About 100 meters north of the shrine lies a granite rock measuring 8 m in length, 7 m in width, and 2 m in height, which is split diagonally in a straight line near the center. According to legend, after losing a match to {{ill|Kamiizumi Nobutsuna|Q1375744|qid=Q1375744}}, Sekishūsai Muneyoshi trained in swordsmanship here every night for three years against {{ill|Tengu|Q742360|qid=Q742360}}. One night, believing he had cut down a tengu with a single stroke, he discovered it was actually this rock, and it is said that the footprints of the tengu remain on its surface <ref>‘History of Nara City: Folklore Volume’. ‘History of Nara Prefecture’, Vol. 13, states that they are claw marks of a tengu.</ref>. Incidentally, through this training, Muneyoshi is said to have realized the ultimate principle of “no-sword” and became the founder of {{ill|Yagyū Shinkage-ryū|Q492116|qid=Q492116}}.

=== Access ===
*From JR {{ill|Nara Station|Q1150978|qid=Q1150978}} or {{ill|Kintetsu Nara Station|Q6414371|qid=Q6414371}}, take a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nara Kōtsū Bus}} bound for Yagyū / Muraji Nakamura for 50 minutes, get off at “Yagyū,” then walk 15 minutes.
